Earth’s gravity is too weak to hold it, so it slowly escapes from the atmosphere into space
Used to pressurize rocket fuel tanks and as a shielding gas in welding

trap.title: Not hydrogen, not neon
trap.body: This element and hydrogen share many clues: the Sun, fusion, balloons, and airships. Hydrogen is the fuel the Sun fuses, while this element is what that fusion makes; hydrogen burned in the _Hindenburg_, while this element fills modern blimps because it cannot burn. Neon and argon are the other traps: they are also unreactive noble gases, used in glowing signs and light bulbs.
trap.fix: Atomic number 2, the yellow line seen during the 1868 eclipse, alpha particles, superfluids, and the lowest boiling point all mean helium. Atomic number 1, the _Hindenburg_, and “water-former” mean hydrogen; glowing red-orange signs mean neon.

topics.name: Distillation
topics.kicker: Separation technique · Boiling a mixture, then condensing the vapor
topics.briefing: Distillation separates the parts of a liquid mixture by boiling it and then cooling the vapor back into a liquid in a separate container. Because each substance boils at its own temperature, the ones with lower boiling points escape first. Oil refineries use giant towers to split crude oil into gasoline, jet fuel, and diesel, and some dry countries use distillation to turn seawater into fresh drinking water.
topics.answerHtml: Distillation (accept distilling; accept specific types such as fractional distillation or steam distillation; prompt on fractionation)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The McCabe–Thiele method uses a graph to estimate how many theoretical plates a column needs to carry out this process. Each theoretical plate stands for one stage in which vapor and liquid reach equilibrium with each other.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique that separates liquids by boiling a mixture and condensing the vapor.

tossups.p: The alchemist Maria the Jewess is credited with inventing the tribikos, a three-armed device for this process, as well as the water bath now called a bain-marie [“ban-muh-REE”]. Alchemists in Roman-era Egypt wrote some of the earliest descriptions of equipment for this process.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ancient technique that separates liquids by boiling a mixture and cooling the vapor.

tossups.p: In a Liebig [“LEE-big”] condenser used for this process, cold water enters the outer jacket at the bottom and leaves at the top, flowing opposite to the hot vapor. The thermometer for this process is placed with its bulb level with the side arm, so it measures the temperature of the vapor.
tossups.r: The purified liquid drips into a receiving flask. For 10 points, name this lab technique that separates a liquid mixture using differences in boiling points.

tossups.p: A Vigreux [“vee-GRUH”] column, a glass tube with many inward-pointing dents, is used in the fractional form of this process, giving rising vapor more surfaces on which to condense and boil again. Each time the vapor condenses and boils again, it becomes richer in the liquid with the lower boiling point.
tossups.r: Oil refineries use tall towers for this process to separate crude oil into gasoline, kerosene, and diesel. For 10 points, name this technique that separates liquids by their boiling points.

tossups.p: Carl von Linde built machines that turned air into a liquid, which could then be separated into nitrogen, argon, and oxygen by the fractional form of this process. Nitrogen comes off first in that separation because it boils at the lowest temperature of the three.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that separates a mixture by boiling it and condensing the vapors.

tossups.p: Perfume makers use the “steam” form of this process to pull fragrant essential oils out of plants like lavender, because steam carries the oils over at temperatures below their normal boiling points. Lowering the pressure in the “vacuum” form of this process lets heat-sensitive substances boil at lower temperatures.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique that separates the parts of a liquid mixture by boiling it and condensing the vapor.

tossups.p: A rotary evaporator quickly removes solvents from a sample using a low-pressure version of this process, spinning the flask to spread the liquid into a thin film. Boiling chips are often added before this process to prevent violent bursts of boiling called bumping.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which a mixture is boiled and its vapor is cooled in a condenser.

tossups.p: Raoult’s [“rah-OOLZ”] law helps explain why the vapor above a boiling mixture is richer in its more volatile liquid, the key idea behind this process. Repeating this process on the collected liquid can make it purer each time.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this separation technique based on differences in boiling points, which uses a condenser to turn vapor back into liquid.

tossups.p: In a refinery tower used for this process, small molecules such as propane rise to the top, while thick, heavy leftovers like asphalt stay near the bottom. Gasoline, kerosene, and diesel are drawn off as separate fractions at different heights in between.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that uses differences in boiling points to separate crude oil and other liquid mixtures.

tossups.p: Multi-stage flash plants in the Middle East turn seawater into fresh water using this process, which leaves the salt behind. A simple solar version of this process lets sunlight evaporate water under a plastic sheet, where the vapor condenses and drips into a cup.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this purification process in which a liquid is boiled and its vapor is condensed and collected.

tossups.p: A Dean–Stark trap uses this process to pull water out of a reaction as it forms, with help from a solvent like toluene that boils off together with the water. In the lab version of this process, vapor travels from a heated flask through a condenser into a receiving flask.
tossups.r: Crude oil is separated into fuels by this technique. For 10 points, name this separation technique based on differences in boiling points.

tossups.p: Medieval chemists in the Islamic world used a device called the alembic to perform this process and make rose water. The alembic’s heated pot held the mixture, while its head caught the rising vapor and sent it down a spout. The word “alembic” comes from Arabic, which took it from Greek.
tossups.r: This technique uses a condenser to turn vapor back into a liquid. For 10 points, name this technique that separates the parts of a liquid mixture by boiling and condensing.

tossups.p: Ethanol cannot be completely separated from water by this process, because the two form a constant-boiling mixture called an azeotrope [“ay-ZEE-uh-trohp”], whose vapor has the same makeup as the liquid. To get pure ethanol, chemists can add a third liquid, such as benzene, that changes how the mixture boils.
tossups.r: Lab glassware for this process includes a heated flask, a condenser, and a receiving flask. For 10 points, name this technique for separating liquids by boiling point.

tossups.p: The simple form of this process works well when two liquids have very different boiling points, but the fractional form is needed when their boiling points are close together. Water purified by this process is used in car batteries and science labs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique that purifies liquids by boiling them and condensing the vapor.

tossups.p: Unlike refluxing, in which condensed vapor drips back into the boiling flask, this process collects the condensed vapor in a separate container. Large columns for this process send part of the condensed liquid back down the column to improve the separation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this technique used to purify water, separate crude oil, and isolate essential oils by boiling and condensing.

Adding a third liquid, such as benzene, helps make pure ethanol

A Vigreux column has inward-pointing glass dents that give the vapor more surfaces
Maria the Jewess is credited with the three-armed tribikos and the bain-marie water bath
Medieval chemists in the Islamic world made rose water with the alembic, a word that came from Greek through Arabic
Carl von Linde built machines that turned air into a liquid so it could be separated
A rotary evaporator removes solvents with a spinning, low-pressure version
A Dean–Stark trap removes water from a reaction with help from toluene
Multi-stage flash plants in the Middle East make fresh water; a simple solar version drips water from a plastic sheet into a cup
Unlike refluxing, where condensed vapor drips back into the flask, it collects the liquid separately; big columns send some liquid back down

trap.title: Whole process, not one step
trap.body: Tossups on this technique are full of its steps, like boiling, vaporizing, and condensing, so players blurt “evaporation” or “condensation.” Those are only parts of the process, and evaporation alone lets the vapor escape instead of collecting it. Other separation methods are traps too: filtration pours a mixture through filter paper, and chromatography separates substances as a solvent carries them along paper or through a column.
trap.fix: If the clues involve boiling points, condensers, fractions of crude oil, or azeotropes, answer distillation; specific types such as “fractional” or “steam” distillation are also accepted. Filter paper means filtration, and spots moving up paper means chromatography.
trap.line: Real answer line: Distillation (accept distilling; accept specific types such as fractional distillation or steam distillation; prompt on fractionation)

topics.name: Boron
topics.kicker: Element 5 · The metalloid behind borax, slime, and heat-resistant glass
topics.briefing: Boron is element number five, a hard, dark metalloid that is never found pure in nature. Its best-known mineral, borax, is used in laundry boosters and is the secret ingredient that turns white glue into stretchy homemade slime. Boron also helps make the heat-resistant glass used in lab beakers, and it keeps nuclear reactors under control by soaking up stray neutrons.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: William Lipscomb won the 1976 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for explaining how compounds of this element and hydrogen are held together by three-center, two-electron bonds. In the simplest of those compounds, two hydrogen atoms form bridges between two atoms of this element.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 5, found in the mineral borax.

tossups.p: Herbert C. Brown shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for using compounds of this element in organic reactions, such as a two-step reaction that adds water across a double bond. Akira Suzuki’s coupling reaction joins carbon atoms using organic compounds of this element and palladium.
tossups.r: This element’s best-known mineral is borax. For 10 points, name this metalloid with atomic number 5.

tossups.p: This element is made mostly when cosmic rays smash larger atomic nuclei in space, rather than by fusion inside stars, which helps explain why it is rare in the universe. Its two stable isotopes have mass numbers 10 and 11.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, the lightest in group 13, which sits just left of carbon on the periodic table.

tossups.p: This element’s isotope with mass number 10 absorbs neutrons so well that the element is used in control rods and dissolved in the cooling water of some nuclear reactors to keep the chain reaction in check.
tossups.r: This element’s carbide is one of the hardest materials known and is used in armor. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 5.

tossups.p: Adding a tiny amount of this element to silicon creates “holes” and makes a p-type semiconductor, because each of its atoms has one fewer valence electron than a silicon atom. It is the only metalloid in group 13.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, whose mineral borax is used in laundry products and homemade slime.

tossups.p: This element’s trifluoride is a classic Lewis acid: its central atom has only six electrons around it, so it eagerly accepts a pair of electrons from ammonia. That flat, triangular molecule is a famous exception to the octet rule.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with three valence electrons, the first member of group 13.

tossups.p: The strongest permanent magnets, used in headphones and electric car motors, are made of neodymium, iron, and this element. This element is also a micronutrient that plants need to build strong cell walls.
tossups.r: This element is a metalloid at the top of group 13. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 5, found in borax.

tossups.p: In the 1880s, teams of twenty mules hauled wagons full of a mineral of this element out of Death Valley, California. One of the world’s largest mines for that mineral is near a California town named after this element.
tossups.r: That mineral, borax, is used in cleaning products. For 10 points, name this metalloid with atomic number 5.

tossups.p: The mineral ulexite [“YOO-lek-site”], a source of this element, is nicknamed “TV rock” because its bundled fibers carry an image from one side of the stone to the other. Turkey holds most of the world’s reserves of this element’s minerals.
tossups.r: This metalloid has atomic number 5. For 10 points, name this element found in borax and boric acid.

tossups.p: Ions containing this element and oxygen link the long molecules in white glue together, turning the glue into stretchy homemade slime. An acid of this element mixed with silicone oil produced the bouncy toy Silly Putty.
tossups.r: This element has atomic number 5. For 10 points, name this element found in the cleaning powder borax.

tossups.p: Compounds of this element give a bright green color to flames; for example, a solution of its acid in methanol burns green. That acid is also a mild antiseptic and a common insect killer used against cockroaches.
tossups.r: That acid is boric acid. For 10 points, name this metalloid with atomic number 5.

tossups.p: In 1808, Humphry Davy in London and the team of Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis Jacques Thénard [“tay-NAR”] in Paris separately isolated this element from its acid. It sits between beryllium and carbon in the second row of the periodic table.
tossups.r: This element’s name comes from the mineral borax. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 5.

tossups.p: Pure forms of this element are built from clusters of twelve atoms arranged in a 20-sided shape called an icosahedron [“eye-koh-suh-HEE-drun”]. This element’s nitride can form a soft, slippery solid nicknamed “white graphite” or a cubic form nearly as hard as diamond.
tossups.r: Slime recipes often use borax, a mineral of this element. For 10 points, name this metalloid, the first element in group 13.

tossups.p: Otto Schott developed a heat-resistant glass containing this element in the late 1800s, and that kind of glass is used for lab beakers because it barely expands when heated. Strong, light fibers of this element are used to stiffen aircraft parts and some sports gear.
tossups.r: This element is never found pure in nature. For 10 points, name this metalloid with atomic number 5, found in borax.

tossups.p: Kernite, a mineral named for Kern County, California, is a major ore of this element. This element’s ground-state electron configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p¹, and its average atomic mass is about 10.8.
tossups.r: Like aluminum below it, this element has three valence electrons. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 5.

trap.title: Element, not borax
trap.body: Many clues about this element are really about its compounds: borax in slime and laundry boosters, boric acid as a cockroach killer, and the twenty-mule teams of Death Valley. Players who blurt “borax” or “boric acid” lose the points, because the question wants the element. Look-alike names are traps too: bromine, barium, and beryllium all start with B, and so does boson, a word from physics.
trap.fix: Atomic number 5, group 13, three valence electrons, “metalloid,” and neutron-absorbing control rods all mean boron (symbol B). Bromine is Br, barium is Ba, and beryllium is Be.

topics.name: Calcium
topics.kicker: Element 20 · The metal in bones, teeth, chalk, and limestone
topics.briefing: Calcium is element number 20, a soft, silvery metal that is never found pure in nature because it reacts with water and air. Its compounds are everywhere, though: chalk, limestone, marble, seashells, and eggshells are all made mostly of calcium carbonate. Calcium is the most common metal in the human body, and about 99 percent of it is stored in your bones and teeth.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Scientists at Dubna, Russia, fired beams of this element’s neutron-rich isotope with mass number 48 at heavy targets to create elements 114 through 118. That isotope and this element’s most common isotope, with mass number 40, are both “doubly magic.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this alkaline earth metal with atomic number 20, found in bones and teeth.

tossups.p: Two strong, dark Fraunhofer lines in the violet part of the Sun’s spectrum, called H and K, are caused by ionized atoms of this element. In a flame test, compounds of this element give a brick-red or orange-red color.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 20, whose carbonate makes up limestone.

tossups.p: Four minerals in a row on the Mohs hardness scale, from gypsum at 2 to apatite at 5, are all compounds of this element. Fluorite, a compound of this element and fluorine, gave the word “fluorescence” its name.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 20, found in milk, bones, and teeth.

tossups.p: When a muscle cell is stimulated, ions of this element flood out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum and bind to troponin, which moves tropomyosin so that myosin can grab onto actin. Ions of this element also trigger the release of neurotransmitters and help blood clot.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, the most common metal in the human body, which is found in milk.

tossups.p: Parathyroid hormone raises the level of this element in the blood, partly by releasing it from bones, while a hormone made by the thyroid gland lowers it. Vitamin D helps the intestines absorb this element from food.
tossups.r: Milk is a good source of this element. For 10 points, name this element, which makes up much of the mineral in bones and teeth.

tossups.p: Before electric lights, theaters lit up actors by heating a block of this element’s oxide in a very hot flame until it glowed brilliant white, which gave us the word “limelight.” That oxide forms when limestone is heated in a kiln, releasing carbon dioxide.
tossups.r: That oxide is called quicklime. For 10 points, name this alkaline earth metal with atomic number 20.

tossups.p: Bubbling carbon dioxide through a clear solution of this element’s hydroxide, called limewater, turns it milky as a solid carbonate forms. Adding water to quicklime makes that hydroxide, also called slaked lime, and releases a lot of heat.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, whose carbonate makes up chalk, marble, and seashells.

tossups.p: In 1669, Rasmus Bartholin described how a clear crystal of this element’s carbonate, called Iceland spar, makes anything seen through it appear doubled. Stalactites and stalagmites in limestone caves are made of that same carbonate.
tossups.r: Seashells and eggshells are made of that carbonate too. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 20.

tossups.p: Old miners’ lamps dripped water onto this element’s carbide to make acetylene gas, which burned with a bright flame. This element’s chloride is spread on icy roads and is used to dry out other chemicals.
tossups.r: Its carbonate is the main part of limestone. For 10 points, name this alkaline earth metal that sits between magnesium and strontium.

tossups.p: In 1808, Humphry Davy isolated this metal by passing electricity through a mixture of lime and mercury oxide, the same year he isolated magnesium, strontium, and barium. This element’s name comes from the Latin word for lime.
tossups.r: Its compounds include chalk and limestone. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 20.

tossups.p: Heating gypsum, a sulfate of this element, drives off some of its water to make plaster of Paris, which hardens again when water is added. Drywall used inside houses is made mostly of that same sulfate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, whose carbonate is the main ingredient in natural chalk and many antacid tablets.

tossups.p: Water rich in ions of this element and magnesium is called “hard” because it makes soap form scum instead of lather. Water softeners swap those ions for sodium ions. The crusty white scale that builds up inside kettles is mostly this element’s carbonate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, which the body needs for strong bones and teeth.

tossups.p: Hydroxyapatite [“hy-DROK-see-AP-uh-tite”], a phosphate of this element, makes up most of the mineral in bones and in the enamel that coats teeth. About 99 percent of this element in the human body is stored in the skeleton.
tossups.r: This element is an alkaline earth metal. For 10 points, name this element found in milk, cheese, and other dairy foods.

tossups.p: This element is the fifth most abundant element in Earth’s crust, but it is never found pure in nature, because the soft, silvery metal reacts with water and slowly gives off hydrogen gas.
tossups.r: Like magnesium, it has two valence electrons and forms ions with a 2+ charge. For 10 points, name this alkaline earth metal with atomic number 20.

tossups.p: The White Cliffs of Dover are made of chalk that formed from the tiny plates of ocean algae called coccolithophores [“kok-uh-LITH-uh-forz”], which build those plates from this element’s carbonate. Corals and clams also build their hard parts from that carbonate.
tossups.r: Ions of this metal help muscles contract. For 10 points, name this element found in limestone, eggshells, and bones.

trap.title: Metal, not its minerals
trap.body: Most clues about this element are really about its compounds: limestone, chalk, marble, gypsum, quicklime, and limewater. Players who answer “limestone” or “calcium carbonate” lose the points when the question wants the element. Its neighbors are traps too: magnesium sits right above it and also makes water hard, and potassium sits just before it on the periodic table.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this element” or “this metal,” say calcium (symbol Ca), even when the clue is about a rock or a compound. Atomic number 20, bones and teeth, muscle contraction, and Humphry Davy in 1808 point here; magnesium is element 12, and potassium is element 19.
trap.line: Real answer line: Calcium (accept Ca; accept calcium ions or Ca2+)
